text: CIS credentials are module-specific, which means choosing one is really choosing which part of the platform you want to be the implementation expert in. This lesson walks through the major specializations honestly, grounded in exactly what this path did and didn't give you real hands-on practice with — not in guesses about which one happens to sound more impressive.

CIS-ITSM covers incident, problem, change, and request — and this path covered it twice, in real depth: Course one built the ITIL foundation, and Course eight had you actually configure ITSM workflows. CIS-Discovery covers CMDB population and Discovery configuration, built in Course nine's CMDB, CSDM, and Discovery content. CIS-CSM and CIS-HR are real, valid specializations — but this path simply doesn't cover Customer Service Management or HR Service Delivery in depth anywhere across its thirteen courses. Being honest about that gap matters more than overclaiming coverage that isn't there.

It's tempting to choose a specialization by guessing which one pays more, but resist that instinct. You don't have reliable, verified module-by-module salary data — anything you've seen quoted online is likely anecdotal, regional, or outdated. More importantly, a CIS credential only has real value once you've actually implemented that module competently, and competence comes from hands-on practice, not from the certificate itself.

So use a practical method instead: look back honestly at your own work across courses one through thirteen. Which module did you spend the most real, hands-on time configuring, not just reading about? Could you walk a technical interviewer through a specific example of what you built, why, and what broke along the way? Does that module's day-to-day implementation work actually match what you'd want to be doing?

For most students finishing this path, that process points honestly to CIS-ITSM or CIS-Discovery, because those are the two modules you got genuine, repeated hands-on exposure to here. If your honest answer points to CSM or HR instead, because of outside interest or a specific target employer, that's a legitimate choice too — it just means starting that module's study closer to the beginning rather than building on depth you already have. Next up: once you've picked a specialization, how to actually prepare for its exam.
